engine


a character, “slopes” or “sandwich”.


sigma


a numeric, the niche bandwidth the fit used.


condition


a character (length 0 or 1), the condition the fit was given (the sandwich engine fits condition-specific slopes only if it was given one; the slopes engine only records it).


patients


a data.frame, one row per patient (sample): its id, the number of cells it contributes, and every colData column that is constant within patients (so a condition can be named at testSpiDE() time).


index


a named list, one element per index cell type, holding the engine’s estimates (see Details).


params


a list of the settings the fit used.

text:
One sample’s cells, coloured by the log1p density of a niche type: the covariate spiDE regresses on. With index, only the index type’s cells are coloured – the covariate as the index type’s model reads it – and the others are dim.   spe,
  niche,
  sample,
  index = NULL,
  sigma = NULL,
  cell_type = "cell_type",
  sample_id = "sample_id",
  section = NULL,
  name = "Niche",
  point.size = NULL,
  scale.bar = TRUE,
  unit = NULL
)

title: The spiDE model
text: In this article we explain what spiDE computes and why, one step at a time. We start each step in plain language and then give the formula, followed by what the formula says in words, so the text can be read with or without the maths. It holds all the statistics of the package, from the model of a single gene to the tests of gene sets and of niche abundance. How to run the functions is in vignette("spiDE"), how well the tests hold up on real and simulated data is in vignette("spiDE-calibration"), and how many patients and cells a study needs is in vignette("spiDE-design").

title: The spiDE model
text:
Within patients: what testSpiDE() tests

A. The same slope in every patient (independent of the condition). Within each patient, the gene rises (or falls) with the density of the niche type, and the patients agree. Patients may differ in their overall level of the gene, as the lines in panel A sit at different heights; that does not matter, because only the slopes are compared. The pooled test detects it (testSpiDE(), then results(res, test = "pooled")). A call means: in the same tissue, index cells with more of this niche type around them express more (or less) of the gene, consistently across patients.
B. A slope that differs between the groups (condition-specific). The slope is present in one group only (panel B), is stronger in one group, or runs in opposite directions. The condition-specific test detects it (testSpiDE(condition = ), then results(res, test = "condition")), as the difference in average slope, second level minus first. A call means: the index cells’ response to each extra unit of niche density differs between the groups.

By default the condition-specific test is run only among triplets that pass one of two filters (see “Multiple testing”): the pooled test, or a test that the slopes vary between patients more than their sampling noise allows. A slope present in one group only, or stronger in one group, has a non-zero average and can pass the first. All three patterns make the slopes vary between patients and can pass the second, including a slope that reverses between the groups and averages out close to zero. To spiDE 0.99.36 only the first filter was used (procedure = "filtered"), so a reversing slope was unlikely to reach the condition-specific test.
A within-patient slope is not always a response of the index cells. Transcripts of neighbouring niche cells can be assigned to index cells when cells are segmented, and they too rise with the niche’s density. plotSpillover() (see vignette("spiDE")) shows whether the calls are the niche type’s own markers.

title: The spiDE model
text:
Between patients: what testNicheAbundance() tests
spiDE’s model gives each patient its own baseline level of every gene (the patient intercepts of Step 2). Everything that differs between patients as a whole is set aside before the slopes are estimated, including a real association: patients whose index cells sit among more of the niche type may express the gene differently overall. testNicheAbundance() asks that question separately, on one pseudobulk profile per patient and index type, against the patient’s mean niche density.

C. Patients with more of the niche differ (independent of the condition). Within each patient the gene is flat, but the patients’ means rise with their mean niche density (panel C). The term "niche" of testNicheAbundance() detects it: across all patients without a condition, averaged over the two groups with one. A call means: patients whose index cells sit among more of this niche type have more (or less) of the gene in those cells.
D. That association differs between the groups (condition-specific). The patients’ means rise with their niche density in one group only (panel D). The term "condition:niche" of testNicheAbundance(condition = ) detects it, as the difference between the groups, second level minus first.

These are statements about patients, not about cells responding to their neighbours. Patients with more of a niche type differ in many other ways too: in their overall composition, in sample quality, or in signal spilling between cells across the whole section. A between-patient association cannot be pinned on the niche, which is why spiDE’s own tests work within patients. Report each result as what it is, and never a result of one test as a result of the other.

title: The spiDE model
text:
What spiDE does not test
Two effects of a condition are absorbed by the patients’ own levels, and no spiDE test looks at them:

E. The gene’s level differs between the groups, whatever the neighbourhood (panel E). This is ordinary differential expression between conditions. Test it on pseudobulk profiles with a differential expression method such as limma or edgeR.
F. The amount of the niche differs between the groups (panel F): a change in tissue composition, here more of the niche type around the index cells of late-stage patients, while expression does not change with it. Test it with a composition method, such as sccomp or speckle for cell-type proportions.

This matters most for a condition such as disease progression, which changes tissue in many ways at once. Most of those changes are differences between patients: late-stage tissue has more of some cell types and less of others (F), and its cells express some genes more or less (E), often both together and often in cell types that interact. Neither is a change in how cells respond to their neighbours, and the condition-specific test sees neither. It sees only a changed response per unit of neighbour density (B): within late-stage tissue, index cells with more niche cells around them differ from index cells with fewer by more, by less or in the opposite direction than within early-stage tissue. A changed interaction between two cell types reaches this test only when it changes that response. “Late-stage tumours have more fibroblasts, and their tumour cells express more of a gene” is F and E, not B, even when both happen in the same patients.

title: The spiDE model
text:
The effects in the model
Reduced to one niche type, with each patient’s niche densities centred at their mean, the model of Step 2 reads, for gene \(g\) in index cell \(i\) of patient \(s\):
\[
\log \mathrm{E}[y_{gi}] \;=\; a_{gs} \;+\; \beta_{gs}\,(\ell_i - \bar\ell_s),
\]
where \(\ell_i\) is the cell’s niche density on the log1p scale, \(\bar\ell_s\) the mean of \(\ell_i\) over the patient’s index cells, \(\beta_{gs}\) the patient’s within-patient slope and \(a_{gs}\) its level at its own mean density. title: The spiDE model
text:
The pooled test
Is the average slope zero? The weighted average of the patients’ slopes is tested with limma’s moderated \(t\)-test. The moderated test borrows information across genes to stabilise each gene’s variance, which helps when patients are few. Two refinements keep it honest:

Borrowing is matched by expression level. A bright gene’s variability is compared with other bright genes, not with the typical gene (eBayes(trend = TRUE, robust = TRUE) on the gene’s log mean expression).
The degrees of freedom count effective patients. When a few cell-rich patients carry most of the weight, the test should not behave as if every patient contributed equally. The Kish effective number of patients, \(n_{\text{eff}} = (\sum_s w_s)^2 / \sum_s w_s^2\), equals the number of patients \(m\) when the weights are equal and falls towards one as they concentrate. The \(t\) statistic is referred to \(\nu_{\text{limma}}
\, n_{\text{eff}} / m\) degrees of freedom (the proportional rule): limma’s degrees of freedom, which include those borrowed from the other genes, scaled by the effective share of the patients. To spiDE 0.99.36 they were \(\min(\nu_{\text{limma}}, n_{\text{eff}} - 1)\) (the capped rule). Since \(n_{\text{eff}} \le m\), that cap always applied and discarded the borrowed degrees of freedom, which made the test conservative with few patients.

title: The spiDE model
text:
The condition-specific test
Does the average slope differ between the two groups? The patients’ slopes are regressed on the condition, with the same weights \(w_{gs}\):
\[
\hat\beta_{gs} = b_0 + \Delta_g\, c_s + [\text{strata}] + \text{error},
\]
where \(c_s\) is 1 for the second condition and 0 for the first. The estimate \(\hat\Delta_g\) is the difference in average slope, second level minus first.
Its standard error does not assume the weights are exactly right. It is a robust (HC2 sandwich) standard error, computed from how far each patient’s slope actually sits from its group’s fit, with small-sample Bell-McCaffrey degrees of freedom. This matters when some patients’ slopes are noisier than their weights suggest. A marker gene that is patchy within the index type is an example: its slope can swing with where the patches fall. Such a patient widens the interval rather than producing a call.
The weights come from the gene-shared variances \(v_{gs}\) and never from a gene’s own tile variance. A gene’s own tile variance, computed at the pooled fit, grows when a patient’s slope sits far from the pooled slope. Weighting by it would down-weight exactly the patients that differ most and shrink the estimated difference toward zero.
strata (a patient-level slide or batch column) adds one term per stratum to the condition model. Use it when the condition is partly confounded with slide, so that slide differences in slope are not read as condition differences. A condition entirely confounded with the strata cannot be tested and is refused.

title: Validation: calibration and accuracy
text:
Can we trust the calls?
A test is only useful if its error rate is what it claims. When spiDE reports a \(q\)-value below 0.05, the expected share of false calls among the calls should be at most 5%. In this article we show how we checked that on real spatial data, where we do not know the truth but can build data in which there is nothing to find, and on simulated data with a known truth, where we can measure accuracy and power. We then report what the checks found for both engines, for the choice of sequencing depth adjustment, for gene sets and for the between-patient test, and we end with what has not been measured.
Together with vignette("spiDE-design"), this is one of the two places in the package that quote benchmark numbers. How many patients and cells a study needs, and the defaults for small studies, are in that article. The statistics are in vignette("spiDE-model"), and the workflow in vignette("spiDE"). The studies behind the numbers are described in (Bhuva et al., in preparation).


How calibration is checked
The idea is to run spiDE on data where, by construction, there is nothing to find, and to see whether it stays quiet. We make two kinds of such null data from each real cohort.
The first is the block null, in which the neighbourhood is scrambled. In every tissue section we shift the niche densities by a random offset, wrapping around the edges, so that each cell receives the neighbourhood of a cell elsewhere in the same section. The niche maps stay as smooth as real ones, but a cell’s expression no longer has anything to do with its neighbourhood. Both the pooled test and the condition-specific test should find nothing. Each shifted map is a full refit.
The second is the permutation null, in which the condition is scrambled. We shuffle the condition labels between patients, within each slide so that a slide difference cannot pose as a condition difference. The niche effects are real, but they no longer differ between the shuffled groups, so the condition-specific test should find nothing.

Sequencing depth
A cell’s library size mixes technical capture with its biological RNA content, and the RNA content can itself depend on the neighbourhood. We therefore judged depth handling by how accurately each option recovered the planted effects, not by how much library-size signal it removed. We compared four options in the simulations above:

one slope on the log library size (depth = "loglib");
a smooth curve in it ("nonlinear");
a library-size effect that varies across the tissue ("spatial_spline");
SpaNorm’s library-size component as a fixed offset.

In the slopes engine the four lay within 0.015 of each other in bias, with the same power, and every one was calibrated in every scenario, so the default is the simplest, "loglib". (The sandwich engine with "loglib" ran wide on GSE289194, up to 1.13.) The spatial option costs a median of 1.2 to 1.8 times as much to fit, per template, in the slopes engine.
One consequence holds for every option. When the neighbourhood raises a cell’s total RNA, adjusting for library size also removes that part of the niche effect, so a pooled slope reports expression relative to the cell’s total RNA. In the simulations this removed most of a niche-driven change in total RNA from the pooled slope. The condition-specific test is affected only by the part of that change that differs between conditions.

What has not been measured
Some questions remain open.

Bandwidth. Each cohort was checked at one bandwidth. Comparing results across bandwidths is a sensitivity analysis, and each bandwidth is its own set of tests.
Many index types at once on small panels. The checks used five index types per cohort. With many more, the pooled test’s multiple-testing burden grows and power falls accordingly, though calibration is not expected to change.
Very small cohorts on real data. The smallest real group checked whole had 9 patients. Smaller designs were checked by subsampling the real cohorts’ patients and simulated down to 6 patients (3 per condition), as described in vignette("spiDE-design"). At 6 patients (3 per condition) the condition-specific test is mostly unavailable. For each gene it needs a Kish effective number of patients, \((\sum w)^2 / \sum w^2\) over that gene’s usable patients’ weights, of at least 3 in each condition. The effective number never exceeds the patient count and equals it only when the weights are equal, so 3 patients in a group pass only if their weights are equal; in practice a group needs more than 3 patients. Genes that fail return NA.

title: R vs Python
text:
We begin with what stays the same. spidepy is a port of spiDE 0.99.37: it runs the same method, the slopes engine and the sandwich engine, the same pooled and condition-specific tests and the same gene-set and abundance tests. A test suite compares spidepy with reference values computed by the R package, and the numbers agree to numerical closeness. The method is defined by the R package, so that is the one to cite.
What changes is the way you call it. Names are snake_case in Python with R’s defaults (min.cells is min_cells), and R’s BPPARAM is n_jobs. Inputs and outputs follow Python conventions:
The two pages below are the package’s own documentation of the correspondence. The first lists every exported R function with its Python counterpart; the second lists the places where the two behave differently, with the reason for each.

title: R vs Python
text:
Interface

AnnData instead of SpatialExperiment. Counts are read from layers[assay] (or X), coordinates from obsm["spatial"], niche matrices live in obsm["Niche<sigma>"] instead of reducedDim, and only _io.py transposes to R’s genes x cells. build_niches and merge_niches work in place unless copy=True (R returns a modified copy).
n_jobs replaces BPPARAM. An integer; the result is identical for any value.
Result tables keep R’s column names. p.heterogeneity and q.global are not renamed to snake_case, so tables from the two packages line up column for column.
spide does not keep the niches it builds. R’s spiDE() returns the results and leaves the caller’s object untouched; spide builds the niche matrix in place (to avoid copying the counts) and removes it from adata.obsm once the fit is done. A niche matrix already present is used and kept.
spiGSEA argument matching. R’s match.arg accepts unambiguous prefixes (type = "self", test = "pool"). spi_gsea takes exact values only, as test_spide does; an unknown value raises ValueError. Also spi_gsea refuses anything but a SpiDEResults with a TypeError (R dispatches and errors on the missing method).
spiGSEA direction of a missing statistic. R writes NA_character_; spi_gsea uses None in the direction column (object dtype).
Result and fit objects. R stores character(0) where Python has None: SpiDEFit.condition when no condition was given; SpiDEResults.condition is None when no condition was tested, and contrast is "" then.
Legacy-object guard. R’s checkResults also rejects pre-0.99.23 mixed-model objects (.assertCurrent). Not ported: spidepy has no such objects.
Strata that vary within a patient. R’s fitSpiDE reads as.character(patients[[strata]]); a strata column that is not constant within patients is absent from the patient table, so R fails with the obscure “‘names’ attribute [n] must be the same length as the vector [0]”. fit_spide raises ValueError("strata column '...' is not a patient-level column") (same for a condition, as R’s .conditionCoding). Same inputs fail in both; only the message differs.

title: R vs Python
text:
Ordering and sorting

Sorting of character labels. R sorts character labels (patients, cell types, conditions) in the session locale (en_US.UTF-8, which interleaves a A b B and ignores punctuation at first pass). spidepy._rcompat.r_sort_str (and Python sorted) uses code-point order (R’s method = "radix" / LC_COLLATE=C), so mixed-case or punctuated labels can order differently (for example b, C in R but C, b here). Labels that share case and punctuation style, such as S1, S10, S2 or Non-responder, Responder, order identically. Code-point order is deterministic and independent of the user’s locale, and it matches the reference fixtures; it is the documented choice rather than emulating glibc collation. Likewise the rows of patient_slopes / patient_intercepts: R sorts rows with order() on character keys (locale collation); Python sorts in code-point order (see “Sorting of character labels”). Identical for labels such as G1, G10, G2, S1, S10, S2.
Niche bandwidth lookup. R finds niche reducedDims with the regex ^Niche[0-9.]+$, which misses a bandwidth that paste0 writes in exponent form (Niche1e+05). _io.niche_keys uses the same pattern, so such a niche is not found either. Matched to R because bandwidths of 1e5 or more are not meaningful in spatial units; niche_key still writes the R string.

title: R vs Python
text:
Niches

Niche kernel density. R densityfun returns the values of in-window queries only (drop = TRUE) and has diggle = FALSE as its own default. _kde.density_at keeps the query order, returns nan for a query outside the window and defaults to diggle = True (the value buildNiches passes). The numbers for in-window queries are identical: spatstat uses the exact pnorm edge weight for a rectangular window, not a pixel image.
merge_niches group named like a leftover column. If a group name equals a column that is not in any group (for example {"B": ["A", "C"]} with a column B), R produces two columns named B and its [[ lookup of the group map sees the first. We keep both columns and record the first in uns["spiDE_niche_groups"] (a dict cannot hold duplicate keys).
merge_niches key prefix. With sigma = None, R greps ^Niche over reducedDimNames, so any key beginning with name (for example NicheFoo) is merged and given a group map, not only Niche<number> keys. merge_niches does the same over obsm keys.

title: R vs Python
text:
Fit: design and slopes

Constant-column test in _niche_columns. R’s var accumulates in long double, so a niche column of identical values has variance exactly 0 and is dropped. _design._colvar does the same (long double, two-pass mean); a plain double mean can leave about 1e-33 and keep the column.
_partial_block singularity. R’s solve fails when the reciprocal condition number of Z'WZ (LAPACK dgecon estimate) is below machine epsilon, and the block is then skipped (NULL). We compute the exact 1-norm reciprocal condition number from the inverse and apply the same threshold; the two can disagree only for blocks within a few percent of that threshold.
r2 of the depth blocks. R uses lm.fit (pivoted QR, tolerance 1e-7) for the R^2 of a niche column on a patient’s block; we use numpy.linalg.lstsq. They agree whenever the block has full column rank (it does for the sections whose df rule applies); a numerically rank-deficient block could drop different directions.

title: R vs Python
text:
limma and empirical-Bayes moderation

fitFDistUnequalDF1 with exactly two informative genes. R sets prior.weights <- NULL after having set its PriorWeights flag, so when NA or tiny-df genes are also present the weighted branch runs on NULL weights: the prior scale is 0/0 = NaN and the objective is identically 0, so optimize returns the value of a flat search. Matched (scale = nan, same df2); the posterior variances are then all nan, as in R.
limma weightedLowess. _limma._weighted_lowess is a port of weighted_lowess.c from limma 3.66.0 (Bioconductor RELEASE_3_22). The window search is vectorised (other points sorted by distance, right side first on ties, then a cumulative sum in the same order of additions) instead of growing the window point by point; results agree with R to rounding, including on tied x. rsort_with_index ties among equal residuals are broken stably (only affects the robustness-iteration median when residuals tie exactly). The equal-weights branch of loessFit (plain lowess) is not ported: it cannot occur from fitFDistUnequalDF1.
eBayes outputs not computed. var.prior, lods and the F statistics (tmixture.matrix, classifyTestsF) are not read by spiDE and are not returned; lmFit’s cat("Coefficients not estimable") message is not printed (aliased coefficients are nan).
Unequal-df prior to ~1e-9. fitFDistUnequalDF1 finds df2 by Brent’s method (R optimize) on a sum that R accumulates in long double and numpy in double, so df.prior agrees with R to about 1e-9 relative, not to machine precision.
Robust fitFDistUnequalDF1 drops span in its refit. R refits with prior weights through Recall(x, df1, covariate, robust = FALSE, prior.weights = FDR), which omits span, so the refit trend always uses the default chooseLowessSpan(n, small.n = 500). We do the same.
Robust fits with tied F statistics. fitFDistRobustly ranks the F statistics for prob.outlier. When a trend interpolates several genes exactly their statistics tie up to rounding noise (about 1e-16) and the ranks, hence prob.outlier and df2.shrunk of those genes, depend on the last bits (R and numpy can differ). Not matched beyond rounding.
qf with log.p. fitFDistRobustly with unequal df1 calls qf(..., log.p = TRUE); scipy has no log-scale quantile, so we use exp(logp) first. Identical unless the tail probability underflows (about 1e-308).
fitFDistRobustly with two variances returns fitFDist’s result without df2.shrunk, as R does; reaching that after set-aside genes fails in R (replacement has length zero) and raises ValueError here.
.pooledColumnTest robust-to-non-robust fallback. R wraps eBayes(robust = TRUE) in tryCatch and, on failure, retries with robust = FALSE. The helper eb() reads the free variable fit, and fit <- eb(TRUE) has just overwritten it with NULL, so the retry runs eBayes(NULL), fails, and the whole column is NA. _pooled_column_test reproduces this: a failed robust prior leaves every row of the column NA (no retry). Unit-tested with a failing e_bayes; no reference fixture reaches it.
Tie noise in limma’s robust prior on small gene families. With a handful of genes whose residuals from the expression trend are exactly zero, their F statistics tie up to rounding (1e-16) and fitFDistRobustly ranks, hence the shrunk prior df, depend on that noise: a 1e-15 relative perturbation of the residual variances moves df.prior of the tied genes by up to 1e-2 in Python, and R’s own value is one such draw. On the end-to-end slopes fixture (toyspe_s16_n150_g12_seed7, index A, niche B, 12 genes) the pooled se/t/df/p differ from R by up to 1e-5 / 1e-3 / 6e-4 although every input to the test is identical to 1e-14. Not fixable (R’s draw depends on its BLAS rounding); tests compare those rows at 2e-2 (0.53% was seen between numpy / BLAS builds).

title: R vs Python
text:
Toy data

Toy-data simulators. R’s .toySPE(), .toyNiche() and .toyClustered() seed R’s Mersenne-Twister; simulate_toy(), simulate_niche() and simulate_clustered() use the same generative model with numpy.random.default_rng(seed), so a given seed gives a different data set from R’s (R’s draws cannot be reproduced). The planted effect is the same but its statistical power is draw-dependent (R’s seed 7 is a favourable draw; here seed 4 is for the same design). Neither touches the global RNG. They return AnnData (the layout load_spe builds from R’s SpatialExperiment) with plain-string sample_id, condition and cell_type and float counts. toy_spide() is R’s own toySpiDE object, not a simulation; its text columns are returned as strings rather than the categories stored in the bundled file.
.toyNiche() and .toyClustered() are gone from R. R dropped the originals of these two internal simulators in c8db60a (the simplification pass). spidepy keeps their ports, simulate_niche() and simulate_clustered(), as public toy-data helpers; they no longer have an R original to be compared with, and simulate_toy() (R’s .toySPE()) is still the one with a counterpart.

title: R vs Python
text:
Plots

Plots return matplotlib figures, not ggplot objects. plot_niche_map and plot_niche_response return a Figure; R’s p$data and layer data are available from the private builders _niche_map_data and _niche_response_data (a dict: data, and summary and lines or centroids), which keep R’s column names, row order and plotmath gene_lab strings. Panels are boxed titles (not full-width strips), legends are two stacked legends placed by hand, and scale_y_log10 labels use a comma for thousands via a formatter; pixel identity is not a goal.
R’s message() in plotNicheResponse. “G2 not fitted in A, left out” is an unconditional message() in R; plot_niche_response emits it as a UserWarning so callers can catch it.
.fmtq pads q = 1. formatC(1, digits = 2, format = "g") returns "  1" (padded to three characters); _fmt_q reproduces it.
Plotted counts are dense. _index_cell_data returns the plotted genes’ counts as a dense genes x cells array (R keeps a sparse subset); only the requested genes are ever extracted.
Italic gene labels. R plotmath (italic("G1")) becomes mathtext ($\mathit{G1}$) with each non-alphanumeric character set in \text{} (a bare - would render as a spaced minus sign), so names with _ - " \ $ { } % # & ^ print as written.
plotPValues row order follows merge()’s unstable tie order. R’s merge(tab, bands, by = c("gene", "index")) sorts the matches of each key with an unstable shell sort (isort_with_index), so the rows of one (gene, index) are not in table order. _isort_with_index reproduces that sort, so p$data has R’s row order; the histograms do not depend on it.
Clustered heatmap rows. hclust(dist(m))$order is reproduced from scipy’s complete-linkage merges (singleton before cluster, lower-numbered cluster first, leaves read left to right); only exact distance ties could differ.
Spillover labels. R places them with ggrepel (seed = 1); matplotlib has no equivalent and ggrepel is optional in R. Labels are right-aligned at log2(fold) - 0.4, pushed apart vertically, with a segment to the point. Which markers are labelled (largest |z|) is R’s.
marker with a missing fold. R’s marker is NA where the fold is NA; here it is False (the fold of a gene is only NA when the gene is missing from the object, which is an error).
Principal-component signs. prcomp and numpy’s SVD may flip a component; only magnitudes (and adjusted R^2, which is sign invariant) are compared with R.
The call graph’s edges. geom_curve(curvature = 0.22) becomes a matplotlib arc3 arrow; the drawn curvature and arrow heads are approximate, the edge data are R’s.
Patient-slope x breaks. R’s scales::breaks_extended(n = 3) (Wilkinson’s extended algorithm) becomes matplotlib’s MaxNLocator(nbins = 3); the tick positions can differ, the plotted values do not.
Spillover threshold label. R nudges it with hjust = 1.05; here it is plainly right-aligned at the fold threshold, so it sits a few points closer to the line.
